channel.title: Keith Dunstan
channel.description: The collected literary works of Keith Dunstan OAM

item.title: On the Wrong Side of Toorak
item.description: A survey of Toorak's transformation from a hilly suburb of large estates and stately homes into a high-rise battlefield, where Whelan the Wrecker demolishes Sir Robert Knox's neo-Tudor mansion, the Nathan Beller 13-storey flat wins Board of Works approval despite 600 protestors in St. John's Hall, and a Bailey bridge over the Yarra triggers Toorak's first public protest movement.

item.title: Paranoia? Call a PAL
item.description: Melbourne in 1969 has become a city of protests on every conceivable subject, from students hanging an effigy of Sir Henry Bolte in the Treasury Gardens to football fans demanding MCG ticket reform, prompting Keith Dunstan to propose Protest Agency Limited, a for-hire service providing professional demonstrators, effigy-makers, slogan-writers, and a wardrobe department, at penalty rates for scuffles with police.

item.title: At Last, a Bridge: Symbol of Natural Modesty
item.description: The West Gate Bridge, costing $42 million and already half finished, gives Melbourne the thumbprint it has always lacked, with its main span of 1000 feet, height of 176 feet above the Yarra's piddling 200 yards, and eight 12-foot lanes quietly surpassing the Sydney Harbour Bridge on every specification except main span length, while Sir Henry Bolte, presented with a silver-plated axe at the 1968 ground-breaking, declared it blunt and denied being a hatchet man.

item.title: You Can't Strike a Good God Down
item.description: The 1969 Melbourne Cup is nearly wrecked when the Railways Union and Tramways Union threaten to stop the special trains and trams to Flemington, the bank clerks call a Monday strike, and the Trades Hall Council places a black ban on all TAB sporting fixtures, until Chief Secretary Arthur Rylah cuts short an oil-rig inspection tour to negotiate a settlement, Sir Paul Hasluck arrives in a Rolls-Royce in top hat and tails, and 85,000 faithful attend the religious festival undisturbed.

item.title: What's His Is Hers and Vice Versa
item.description: Keith Dunstan investigates Melbourne's bisexual fashion revolution at the Myer In Gear shop in Lonsdale Street, where boys buy girls' clothes and girls buy boys' clothes, Nehru jackets and cufflinks are interchangeable, and the only reliable way to tell the sexes apart is by hair length.

item.title: At Last, the Dance Is Over at St. Kilda
item.description: The burning of the St. Kilda Palais de Danse at Christmas prompts a history of Melbourne's famous dance hall, from its controversial opening in 1913 — when 700 protesters condemned the tango as inflaming animal passions — through the great American bands of the twenties and the eventual reign of wedding receptions and Miss Australia presentations.

item.title: The Leisure Rat-Race Is Merciless
item.description: Keith Dunstan's theory that automation and the do-it-yourself movement are inseparable — the more technology does for us, the more we exhaust ourselves laying our own floor tiles, papering our own walls, and pouring our own concrete — developed after five weeks' holidays left him paint-stained and chisel-scarred.

item.title: Again, It's Time for Change in the Name of Charity
item.description: Keith Dunstan reports on the Melbourne walkathon from the city to Frankston, a 25-mile endurance march that raised $50,000 for charity through the cunning sadism of sponsor-per-mile pledges, as limping walkers including Herb Elliott stumbled into the Frankston Life Saving Club at 3 a.m.

item.title: There's Gold in Them There Cans for Cats and Canines
item.description: The Australian pet food market has more than doubled in three years, with over a million tins sold every week, a fact Keith Dunstan discovers at his supermarket's 30-item dog bar, while witnessing the spectacular launch of Lassie dog food at Le Chateau Restaurant complete with a potted stage musical and a $3000 TV commercial featuring a skateboarding dog.

item.title: Thirsting for Spirits in the Theatre
item.description: Since Melbourne theatres won the right to apply for liquor licences in 1966 and not one has done so, Keith Dunstan mounts a campaign against the deliberate cruelty of watching four hours of Dylan Thomas drinking himself to death, the entire cast of 'The Season of the Seventeenth Doll' drinking real Carlton beer, and Ray Milland being driven to ruin by the banquet scene in La Traviata.

item.title: Rolling Along with a Major Revival
item.description: Keith Dunstan visits the Orchestrelle company in Collins Street to find 1500 pianola rolls from a Toorak estate on sale, and reports on the major revival of player pianos since 1961, with Beatles hits and 'Sound of Music' rolls competing alongside vintage duo-art rolls that reproduce Rubinstein exactly, and one Sydney lady who owns three electric-player grands.

item.title: A Visit to Beef Up the Japan Tourist Trade
item.description: The Australian Tourist Commission brings three Sumo wrestlers to Australia, led by grand champion Taiho, who earns $100,000 a year and at six-foot-three and 316 pounds demolishes a banquet at the Sukiyaki Restaurant in Alfred Place with methodical dignity, buying koala bears and boomerangs before departing for home.

item.title: The Wedding, the Greatest Thing Since the Bogle Case
item.description: Keith Dunstan covers the Zara Holt wedding at Millicent Avenue, Toorak, a press circus of 62 journalists, live television cameras, uninvited spectators climbing through windows, and the great friesian calf Meadow Glen Dame Zara afflicted with dissipated dyspepsia — all presided over by Nicky Holt in a four-inch tie.

item.title: Kicking Around the Idea of a Footy Supermarket
item.description: The Victorian Football League's 1930 Coulter Law forbids the sale of players while the trade goes on regardless — North Melbourne reportedly paying $2000 for a Box Hill centreman — leading Keith Dunstan to propose a used-footballer market modelled on American baseball, where entire teams are owned by millionaires and Dalgety's could auction the top players.

item.title: A Reserve Ticket on MacArthur's Bed for Muggeridge
item.description: The four-day auction of the Menzies Hotel's 4000 lots by closed-circuit television, covering twin beds slept in by General MacArthur, Danny Kaye and Sophie Tucker, a $35,000 Czech chandelier, chamber pots with scroll work, the two statues Prudence and Phoebe separated after 102 years, and a bottle of Bass ale from 1902 that nobody thought worth opening for 67 years.

item.title: BHP Leads the High-Rise Trend
item.description: BHP unveils its planned 41-storey tower on the Menzies Hotel site, designed by architect Barry Patten as a severe black-glass building in formal dark suit to contrast with the Hawaiian-shirt towers around it, with a heliport on the roof and natural gas providing a total energy system, part of the greatest wave of high-rise building Melbourne has ever seen.

item.title: But Will Squizzy's Re-Run Be a Long Run?
item.description: Nigel Buesst's $2000 documentary film on Squizzy Taylor opens at the Carlton cinema, drawing on old photographs, cartoons, and interviews to portray Theodore Joseph Leslie Taylor as a blackguard, flashy dresser, and public-relations genius who outwitted Melbourne police for ten years before dying in a 1927 gunfight with Sydney criminal John D. Cutmore.

item.title: Italy in Suburbia
item.description: Melbourne has become one of the major Italian cities of the world, with 200,000 first- and second-generation Italians, over 500 Continental delicatessens, Italian-language cinemas in Footscray and Ascot Vale, and an estimated one million gallons of home-made wine produced annually in backyards from Carlton to Reservoir from grenache and muscatel grapes trucked from the Murray.

item.title: Going to Market About an Adopted Young American
item.description: East Burwood's new K-Mart, the first Australian outpost of the American Kresge Company's discount chain, opens to 5000 customers on its first morning, offering 50 departments and 40,000 items under one vast roof, complete with no-frills pricing, buzzer-controlled lavatories, and a smoking ban copied directly from the American originals.

item.title: This Ozone by Any Other Name Would Smell More Sweet
item.description: Mayor John Staughton's $30,000 promotion campaign to revive St. Kilda's image as a cosmopolitan resort, complete with 4000 colour brochures comparing it favourably to the French Riviera, prompts Keith Dunstan to point out the suburb's unidentifiable patron saint and suggest it needs a new devastating name to rival Surfers Paradise.

item.title: My Wordy Reunion with the Instant Opinion Machine
item.description: Malcolm Muggeridge visits Melbourne to commune with Barry Jones and Hector Crawford, dispensing opinions at his customary rate — Australia is doomed, California and Scandinavia are both like hell, Parliament will be killed by television — while the vegetarian ascetic finds unexpected rapport with fellow non-drinker Barry Jones, though neither can warm to Marshall McLuhan.

item.title: The Red Baron Goes to Battle Again
item.description: The Anti-Football League's latest campaign enlists Robert Joyce's skywriting plane, the Red Baron, to write the AFL battle cube and the letters AFL in half-mile smoke at 12,000ft above Melbourne's six simultaneous football grounds, only for the 50-knot wind to carry the message out beyond Dandenong to be seen by sand-belt golfers rather than MCG pie-eaters.

item.title: Where Culture Reigned and Thunder Rumbled
item.description: The 1969 Moomba festival's bid for culture collapses with a $10,000 balloon that bursts twice, threatening letters and egg-throwing threats against Italian opera star Tito Gobbi as Moomba King, and a Sydney Symphony Orchestra concert attended by fewer people than the ABC's Melbourne typists, while Keith Dunstan reveals that 'moomba' likely means 'thunder' in the Dippil Aboriginal language.

item.title: Save Matilda — Write a Verse and Earn a Guinea
item.description: With Australia still without an official national anthem, Keith Dunstan surveys the shortcomings of the four competing songs — 'Advance Australia Fair,' 'God Save the Queen,' 'Song of Australia,' and 'Waltzing Matilda' — and launches a reader competition offering a guinea prize for the best new verse added to 'Waltzing Matilda.'

item.title: Middle-Aged and Methodist Amidst the Nakedness
item.description: The Melbourne opening of the musical Hair, after producer Harry Miller won approval from Chief Secretary Willis to stage it with full nudity intact, prompts Keith Dunstan's report on the audience in fur and chainmail, the show's sex, blasphemy, and four-letter words assessed from a Methodist-raised vantage point, and the aftermath party at the Chevron where Graham Kennedy's gift of a Rolls-Royce was the talk of the night.

item.title: Could Enzymes Lift That Veil off Dull Elections?
item.description: The proliferation of mystery ingredients in household products — Puradent, Hexachlorophene, Gardol, Enzolve, Politogene — leads Keith Dunstan to propose that the Labor, Country, and Liberal parties adopt the same scientific marketing language for the coming election, with Politogene, deep-acting enzymes, and OK-100-15 as their respective selling points.

item.title: Mirror, Mirror on the Wall, Who's the Most Perverted of Us All?
item.description: Melbourne's Vice Squad charges the cast of Boys in the Band with obscene language and the Customs Minister Senator Scott bans Stig Bjorkman's film 'I Love, You Love,' provoking a film-festival seminar at the Palais Theatre where psychologist John Cowl, novelist David Martin, and broadcaster Corinne Kirby argue that obscene material does not corrupt and that the real censorship problem is Australia's broader pattern of repression.

item.title: When the Queuing Has to Stop
item.description: This year's MCG grand-final ticket queue disintegrates at 2 a.m. in a fist-fight that sends eight people to hospital and leaves two days of bottles and rubbish to clean up, reviving the annual question of whether tickets should be sold by mail, handed to clubs for distribution among worthy members, or — Keith Dunstan's modest proposal — by broadcasting all finals from a secret location in Alice Springs on coaxial cable.

item.title: If You Can't Beat Them in the Search, Join Me in Research
item.description: The arrival of Hong Kong flu prompts Keith Dunstan's Batman White Paper on the winter disease, tracing its escalating nomenclature from Asian flu through Russian flu to the present, noting research scientists' consistent inability to find a cure, and contrasting their diffidence with the supreme confidence of Mrs. Beeton and the 1836 'Magazine of Domestic Economy,' whose cures involved turpentine flannels, garden snails, and stream frogs.

item.title: The Queue — A Kind of Cherished Tradition
item.description: Melbourne psychologist Leon Mann, now lecturing at Harvard, publishes his research on Melbourne's football-final ticket queues, finding that 25,000 people once waited a full week in mud for 12,500 tickets, that veterans regard queuing as a cherished ritual earning Agincourt-level kudos, and that organised scalpers flew Tasmanian students to Melbourne at $1 an hour to stand in line before reselling tickets at $35 apiece.
